sections.COMMENTS:
The Calabrian Arc represents a portion of the complex plate boundary between the Eurasia and Africa plates that formed as a consequence of the subduction of the Ionian oceanic crust underneath the southern margin of the European plate (Calabrian subduction interface). It unfolds between the Tyrrhenian Sea (to the east) and the Ionian Sea (to the west) and stretches for about 300 km between the Southern Apennines (to the north) and Sicily (to the south-west).
The subduction of oceanic crust appears to be still active only in a narrow portion of the Calabrian Arc, near its southwestern end, between the Catanzaro Straits (to the north) and the Messina Straits (to the south), where a steep NW dipping Wadati-Benioff zone can be recognized (Selvaggi and Chiarabba, 1995, Neri et al., 2009; Maesano et al., 2017).
To the north, although convergence is still active, the sedimentary cover of the African continental margin has been wedged into the Calabrian Arc and thrusted towards the foreland, which in turn is possibly involved in the development of compressional structures (Ferranti et al., 2014; Volpi et al., 2017).
To the south, the Calabrian subduction interface is confined by the lateral tear represented by the NW-SE striking Alfeo fault system (Gutscher et al., 2016, 2017; Maesano et al., 2020 and references therein).
Down-dip, the Calabrian subduction interface is characterized by a slab window (Faccenna et al., 2007) and by an incipient slab tear (Maesano et al., 2017) at 70 km depth, which separate the northern detached slab from the southern, still continuous one.
Seismic profiles across the Ionian Sea highlight the thrust structure of the eastern margin of the Calabrian Arc and of the accretionary south-east verging wedge that spans into the Ionian Sea for about 300 km (Minelli and Faccenna, 2010; Polonia et al., 2011; Maesano et al., 2017). The Calabrian subduction zone is also characterized by an active back-arc basin in the Tyrrhenian Sea, related to the pulse-like retreat of the Calabrian slab toward SE that started on late Miocene.
According to GPS velocities and current plate block-models, relative motion between the subducting Africa plate and the Calabrian Arc results in a convergence rate of 2-5 mm/y (D'Agostino and Selvaggi, 2004; Serpelloni et al., 2010; Devoti et al., 2011; Dâ€™Agostino et al., 2011).
Shape and depth of the Calabrian subducting slab or, more in general, of the contact between the two plates, are constrained by gravity, seismic and tomographic data, as well as seismicity data.
The geometry of the uppermost 18 km of the subduction interface is constrained by the interpretation of seismic reflection profiles (Van Dijk et al., 2000; Finetti, 2005; Scrocca et al., 2005; Minelli and Faccenna, 2010; Pepe et al., 2010; Maesano et al., 2017).
In the Ionian Sea, this portion of the plate contact dips toward north-west about 2-8 degrees under the accretionary wedge and it is characterized by an outer flat located below the post-Messinian evaporitic wedge (Polonia et al., 2011; Gallais et al., 2013; Gutscher et al., 2016, 2017; Maesano et al., 2017), a central ramp and a more internal flat which steepens (up to 20 degrees) below 15 km. The subduction interface, which is assumed to operate by nearly pure thrusting and represents the region where interface earthquakes took place, is located between 9 and 34 km on the basis of regional thermal and rheological models (Gutscher et al., 2006) referred to the location of the 150Â°C and 350Â°C isotherms and considering also the depth of slab intersection with the Tyrrhenian Moho.
The geometry of the slab down to 50 km depth is inferred from wide angle seismic profiles (Dellong et al., 2019), P-waves velocities (Di Stefano et al., 1999), residual topography (Gvirtzman and Nur, 2001), gravity anomalies (Tiberti et al., 2005) and paleomagnetic data (Cifelli et al., 2007; Mattei et al., 2007; Cifelli et al., 2008). Earthquake locations are consistent with the slab geometry model derived from other data (ISIDe Working Group, 2007).
The deeper portions of the subduction interface were constrained by tomographic data (Barberi et al., 2004; Chiarabba et al., 2005; Chiarabba et al., 2008; Neri et al., 2009; ScarfÃ¬ et al., 2018), SKS splitting (Baccheschi et al., 2008; Baccheschi et al., 2011), and seismicity distribution (Maesano et al., 2017). Deep seismicity and tomography data depicts a well-developed subduction slab down to 500 km depth.
While intraslab seismicity of the Calabrian Arc is abundant and well documented, seismic coupling values are not available in the literature for the Calabrian subduction interface, due to the lack of well constrained seismic events for the region (Heuret et al., 2011). Numerical modelling of GPS velocities in the area suggest that the Calabrian subduction interface could be partially locked (Carafa et al., 2018).
In the past few centuries, the area has been struck by several M>6 earthquakes. The largest ones include the 28 December 1908 Stretto di Messina event (Mw 7.1), that was caused by a normal fault in the Messina Straits (Valensise and Pantosti, 1992). Another large earthquake took place on 5 February 1783 Calabria Meridionale (Mw 7.1) in southern Calabria (Pizzino et al., 2004). Also, another event has occurred on 8 September 1905 (Mw 7.0; Rovida et al., 2021). Although the latter earthquake is not directly related to the subduction plane, it has been hypothesized that it has occurred within the subduction slab (Presti et al., 2019).
